Today, we have the privilege of witnessing history unfold right before our eyes. While many people will celebrate the title that you have earned, we want to celebrate the heart that you had long before you were seated. segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin

segments.text: Item 73, proposed ordinance asking electors to amend section 7.07 to allow City Council to initiate midyear budget changes without the need for mayoral recommendation and in a manner consistent with general law, providing an effective date.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Thank you. Council have any questions?

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: Yes. We had a global pandemic that no one was expecting. You had to make a lot of changes. Things shut down. It was extraordinary circumstances. By doing this, my question to council, to initiate midyear budget changes, what if something happens that's catastrophic and we're short of funds, how do you feel about that? Would we be spending more than we should and putting ourselves in a position, we have future -- putting a future council in the position, well, we made all these budget changes early on, now we have a crisis, we have to dip into the reserves, what do we do from there? I'm saying, like, just because you can spend it doesn't mean you should spend it.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Councilwoman Young and then Councilwoman Hurtak.

segments.speaker: Naya Young
segments.text: So I had an opportunity to attend some of the negotiations for Tampa fire. With this charter amendment, let's say they come to resolution, comes to council, let's say, we're like, no, that doesn't work. Would this impact that? Like, they would have to go back to the table? What would be the process for that? I was just thinking about that because I know that was, you know --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Let me let Councilwoman Hurtak speak and then I'll respond.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Honestly, yeah. We're in charge of the budget ultimately. But the problem is, once the budget passes, we can't do anything about it. Like, we're not allowed. So we passed a budget in September. We can't make any changes to that. We're not allowed. All changes have to come from the mayor. That's what this change is. This allows us to make changes to the budget. If we see something, say there's something with a park that has a big problem and we're hearing from our constituents that they want it fixed right then, we can actually look at the budget, move some things around, if the administration is like we don't have money for that, we can say, oh, we'll find the money and we can do that. Right now, we don't have that ability. Right now, everything has to go through the mayor and the mayor has to be the one to bring it to us. That's the only way we can approve or deny. That would have nothing to do with it. The administration, when they go into negotiation, what they have done is they have always held the money and assumed that it will pass. If it doesn't, they will reallocate it. For all of the different unions, that's what they have done.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: I'll give you a real-time example. This last budget cycle, and I totally understood why, but why this council didn't buy into it, we were anticipating the potential passage of amendment 3. The administration, remember the controversy about them underrepresenting revenue and sandbagging and underrepresented it, well, that sounded like on the surface a good fiscal policy. But the problem, what we're bound by, by the charter now, by doing that, council gave away their responsibility for the budget. Because we couldn't, like, let's say the situation is reversed. We have another pending something happens with the budget. We want to be fiscally responsible and fiscally prudent. If we don't have this ability, we give away our authority of having budget authority. Because once we pass it, we no longer control the budget. If we were able to say, you know what, the beginning of the fiscal year, I think we're going to leave a hundred million dollars set aside in a pot for the just in case. We can't do that because if we do that, we no longer control that hundred million dollars. If we had ability like this, we could say, you know what, this idea in the beginning of a fiscal year, this idea is not really fully baked yet. Maybe come July when we have more information or come June when we have more information, we're going to put this money here and then in July let's revisit how we'll spend the money. This gives us the ability to do that. Councilwoman Hurtak? Councilwoman Lockett.

segments.speaker: Robin Lockett
segments.text: So I have a question. So what happens now when the budget passes and you're saying that, so once the budget passes you have no more authority.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: We have one bite at the apple.

segments.speaker: Robin Lockett
segments.text: Okay. So if this passes and let's say you have the authority to create or do something different, doesn't the mayor still have the power to -- doesn't the mayor still have power to move it or not.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Robin Lockett
segments.text: So who moves it? She is the administration.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: The mayor would still under this have the same authority tomorrow that they have today. Council would just have additional authority to be able to -- right now what happens is, for robin, since you are new at this. Hadn't gone through a budget cycle with us. Council works on the budget. The mayor prepares an initial presentation and then they wash their hands of it. They hand it to the council. Now we have hundred percent control of that at the end of this fiscal year, we'll have hundred percent control of that. When we pass a budget, we hand it back to the mayor. Now they have, if they want to make changes, let's say there's additional revenue sitting in a pot, if they want to change it, if we see the revenue is there, we can't say, we can't by council motion say I see that there is an extra $20 million in this pot, we should invest this in this park. We have to go to the mayor and have them initiate that budget amendment. We don't have the authority by charter to do that. This would give us the authority to initiate it. Now, the mayor could still veto and we'd have to override. It basically provides that, again, check and -- a balance between the two branches of government by providing this opportunity. I'll go back to the same example. Let's say the clerk, tonya's position, let's say council had to hire that. We set our budget in October and then that position empties in February or march and we don't have the money in our budget, we don't have the ability to initiate a budget amendment to add money to be able to hire that person. By doing this, we do.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: Yeah, so --

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: When she finishes.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: What I was going to say is we actually -- well, I started something a few years ago where the money that we have at the end of 2026 will be coming back to us, and they'll come to us with a report in January to say, hey, this is the money we had left over in 2026. And then council kind of talks about how they would like to spend it. All we can do is do a request for the mayor to spend the money the way we ask. It doesn't have to happen. She doesn't have to agree to it. Even though there's money left over and we're the ones that are bound to spend it, we don't have the ability to move that money to where we want to go. The administration has to approve it. So this would allow us in January to say, hey, this is the money that's left over. This is where we want to go. Boom, done.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Councilman Miranda and then Councilman Carlson.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: A couple of little things here, first of all, the mayor prepares a budget for the coming year of '28. 2027 for '28, usually august, September. Has to be done by September 30, approved and sealed because that's when the next year changes. So that's the mayor's budget. After that is compiled and they do call you in, I've been involved, you go over the finance office and they tell you exactly how it is. That's number one. Number two, after that process, then the mayor brings a budget to the council in one way or another and it becomes the council's budget. Then we do that budget whatever we feel is necessary. The mayor is not involved technically. However, then, here is where the thing is. And, by the way, I almost begged this council not to get involved on anything regarding anything, whatever it was until the vote was taken and you can check the record, on the 3rd of November. They turned it down 4-3. That's why we have the problem we have today. We have a commitment that we can't meet, obligation financially. That's all I'm going to say. So the mayor's budget, in my mind, if we go with this, we're changing the form of strong mayor government through something less than the strong mayor government. So who is going to be the mayor? The council or the person elected mayor? We have a judicial responsibility for financial and other obligation to reject or approve whatever is done in the other house. That's what we do. We either approve it or we start something and we approve it, send it over for confirmation, so forth and so on. I'm not going to support this. I think this weakens a system of the strong mayor and you can't have eight people running a city. You can't have eight people running any business. One has got to be responsible for it with the seven others in support or in rejection of what that one wants. That's all I got to say.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Councilman Carlson.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: As I said in the beginning, I think there needs to be more collaboration. The charter clearly sets up two equal powers. It doesn't reference strong mayor at all in it. And there's no reason for the one body to be stronger than the other. But we have seen in the last 15 years, last two administrations, they usurp the power of City Council and we need to balance it. By coincidence, I've run in different parties, I've run into three different former mayors in the last few days, and all of them talked about how they would pick up the phone and have conversations and collaborate. The last two mayors have chosen not to do that. And so what this does is it forces collaboration in case we get another mayor that doesn't want to do it.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Can I respond and it will be the last word? Councilman Miranda, I think that, one, I don't think it changes balance. There would still be a process where this council Will vote, and we vote, it goes to the mayor. She can veto. We still have that check and balance with this. There's still a check and balance. So all this does is, again, I'm not -- I think as Councilwoman Hurtak alluded, post-cycle money and stuff, we have had some collaborative relationships with how the stuff has been done and we've done it with handshake deals. The administration has been relatively forthcoming and worked well with this council in how we disposed of excess money or shifted money from pots to pots. In fact, we go through this agenda item -- these agenda items today, every week we are moving tens, if not hundreds of thousands, sometimes millions of dollars between budgets. And that's all done by one person. That's all done by the mayor moving money -- constant movements of money. I don't necessarily think that it is a bad thing. Again, find me another solution. If tonya left tomorrow and the clerk was not able to fund that position, and we didn't have the budget within our council budget that we passed on October 1st, there's no other way for me to fund that position without an ability. Let's just say the mayor -- I know it's shocking to think that sometimes the mayors don't like council. But let's say they are, there's no way for me to fund that position without this ability. Councilwoman Lockett.

segments.speaker: Robin Lockett
segments.text: I'm a process person. I'm curious about the process. You find money. You want something done. The administration has to enforce it, right? She still has the power to do it or not. How will she be -- because we will be running around circles because we said, oh, we found a million dollars and we want sidewalks. And then she doesn't implement it. You hear that, you hear all these things now. You find it, she still has the authority to implement it or make it happen. So how would that happen?

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: We can't make her do anything. We can't make her implement. We fight that all the time. All you have to do is look at fire station 24. But, from the dais, we're saying this is important to us, we're going to keep our eye on it. And the public wants it. So we don't generally do anything up here that we haven't heard from the public about. So the public can put their focus and push on the mayor, too. But it really doesn't matter because, again, we can approve a budget that has money in it that we want and she won't use it. That doesn't change that. This just changes our ability, like he said, for things that we do control. So we do control the City Council budget. We do control things like that. But this would say, if we're hearing from the people that they want this park fixed, something like that, we can actually put the money there. The mayor doesn't have to spend it, but then the mayor is the one that gets stuck with the bad press for not doing the park that the people asked for. So there's some pressure there.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin

While I respect your right to express concerns about these proposals, I must take strong exception to both the premise and the implications of your memorandum. Tampa City Council has followed the procedure established by the city charter. A governing document approved by the voters of Tampa. This is not -- this has not been rushed, arbitrary or careless exercise. The Charter Review Commission conducted its work pursuant to the process established by our charter. Its members devoted considerable time and effort reviewing proposals, evaluating their merits and considering the future structure of our municipal government. City Council has taken its responsibility equally seriously. We retained independent legal counsel specifically to assist council in evaluating these proposed charter amendments. That council has thoughtfully reviewed the proposed changes. The legal implications and relationships to the existing charter. In addition, some of our city attorneys have participated in reviewing and evaluating these proposals. These amendments have not been developed in a legal vacuum. They have been subjected to a deliberate process involving the Charter Review Commission, an independent legal counsel, city attorney staff and the elected members of this City Council. Frankly, I take great offense at the implication that City Council, the members of our Charter Review Commission, or the attorneys who have advised us have somehow been negligent in carrying out our responsibilities. Your memorandum repeatedly calls for legal reviews, fiscal evaluations, and operational assessments in a manner that suggests that these matters have been ignored or that the individuals entrusted with this process have failed to exercise their appropriate diligence. That characterization is neither fair nor warranted. The members of the Charter Review Commission deserve recognition for their public service, not an implication that their work was inadequate. Our independent legal counsel and city attorney staff deserve respect from our professional judgment, not an implication that their legal review was insufficient and simply because the administration disagrees with the proposals. The members of council deserve acknowledgment that we have exercised our responsibilities in accordance with the very charter we have been sworn to uphold. A disagreement over public policy does not constitute a failure of due diligence, nor does the administration's opposition to a proposed amendment establish that that amendment is legally deficient, fiscally irresponsible, or procedurally improper. We welcome legitimate questions and constructive recommendations. We've never suggested that the proposed charter amendment should be exempt from legal scrutiny or thoughtful consideration. But we will not accept the suggestion that this process must begin again simply because the administration is dissatisfied with the outcome. There is also an important distinction that should not be lost in this discussion. The Charter Review Commission serves as an important advisory function. City Council has its own responsibility and authority under the charter and state law. The fact that council may reach a different conclusion from the commission on a particular proposal does not diminish the commission's work or invalidate council's judgment. That is how the process is designed to function. The charter does not require unanimity between the mayor, City Council, and the Charter Review Commission before the voters -- before the voters may be asked to consider changes to their government. And that brings us to the fundamental issue. This city charter belongs to the people of Tampa. It does not belong to the mayor. It does not belong to the administration, and it does not belong to this City Council. The voters approved the process by which the charter may be reviewed and amended. We have followed that process. Now, having exercised our responsibilities, we believe the voters should have the opportunity to exercise theirs. These proposed amendments are not about strengthening checks and balances -- I'm sorry -- these proposed amendments are about strengthening checks and balances, establishing meaningful accountability, protecting the independence of the legislative branch, and ensuring that no single branch of municipal government exercise authority without appropriate oversight. They are not an attack on the mayor of this office. I'll go off script for a second. The mayor and I have a working relationship. This is not an attack on the mayor or the mayor's office. They are an acknowledgment of a fundamental principle of american government. Power should never be concentrated that exercising it -- those exercised in it are effectively insulated from independent oversight. The administration is entitled to oppose these amendments. It's entitled to advocate against them, and it is entitled to explain to the public why it believes the existing government structure should remain unchanged. What it should not do is characterize a duly authorized carefully considered and legally reviewed charter amendment process as inadequate merely because the resulting proposals would establish additional checks on executive authority. Our responsibility is not to protect the institutional power of an elected official, including ourselves. Our possibility is to protect the integrity of our government and the rights of the people represent. The mayor has a voice in the debate. City Council has a voice in the debate. segments.text: We are scheduled to come before council in January with the results of last fiscal year. It takes weeks and weeks and weeks to close the books and figure out what happened. As a lead-in to what we're doing right now, I do want to share with you, again, we remain in a very strong financial position, and that's good. That allows us to rebound and plan on ahead. To put it simply, you got two main levers. Revenues coming in and you have expenses going out. From an expenses going out perspective, many of us have been here before. The great financial crisis, the pandemic. And many of the leadership here, council members, we've weathered a similar storm. Hopefully it won't be that bad. We've done it before. We'll do it again. What's that going to entail -- the largest, and you heard us say this before, the largest recurring expense in the city is typically personnel. We're going to look at personnel. Now many, or almost all of the dozens and dozens of position requests in the current year budget that were not approved are going to help us out tremendously from a bottom line perspective. Again, it was a sustainment budget. There were dozens of requests for new positions to expand services. We haven't done that. From an operating expense perspective, review of our contracts, our obligations going forward. Again, we're a big city. segments.text: We don't have the power.

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: So a few weeks ago, I brought up, some individuals from the public regarding -- it's a Florida affordable energy resolution, basically regards to higher electric bills and whatnot. Instead of just making a motion, I passed it around to council members to take a look at it. If council, like a straw poll, if they had the stomach to pursue something like that, if they would be interested instead of putting anybody on the spot, okay, vote it up or down. However, we had a policy we brought up a while ago, if it's not related to city business, that's outside the city's purview, because we don't regulate electricity bills. Public service commission at the state level. That was it.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Councilman Miranda.

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: I understand and have compassion for that. But the city is in the same spot the individuals are. When they raise the rates, they raise our rates. You know how much dollars a day the city uses for electricity? $70,000 a day electric bill. We are in the same boat they are.

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: I know that this evening at 6:30 at the NAACP, TECO is having, there is a community meeting, and TECO is presenting us what they are doing, opening it up for people in the community to ask their questions, bring their utility bills, rate reductions they are doing. I know they are being proactive in that case, but that was it, if there's no appetite for it, we just leave it.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Background, give you background --

segments.speaker: Robin Lockett
segments.text: I'm familiar with it.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: How we got here was there were issues with let's say Cuba. Issues with Cuba, which we don't control foreign policy. There were issues with -- there's a whole bunch of issues, Israel and gaza and things that we have no control over. So we as a council decided that we have a City Council rule that if it's not within our control, if I can't pass an ordinance or pass control in that issue it would be inappropriate for us to have those motions or have that business, take time out of our schedule. We know our lane and stay in our lane and do the stuff we control. Let the legislature and let the congress and the president and do all the stuff they do.

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: I've written letters to the public service commission. Instead of approving rate hikes and rate increases that they be mindful of working people.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Doesn't preclude us from being individual activists.

segments.speaker: Robin Lockett
segments.text: My question is, is the resolution asking you to do something or is the resolution asking to you just confirm or just acknowledge that the rates are too high.

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: Making a statement.

segments.speaker: Robin Lockett
segments.text: Again, a statement is one thing, but in regards to just showing support for constituents. I'm coming from the organizing community aspect of it.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: We'd have to change our rules.

segments.speaker: Robin Lockett
segments.text: The rule is in writing?

segments.speaker: Robin Lockett
segments.text: One suggestion, when these individuals come to you individually --

segments.speaker: Robin Lockett
segments.text: That's not what they are saying. If you are, he wouldn't be bringing it up here. They've had meetings with you guys.

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak
segments.text: We say it to them every time.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: The most recent was the Israel stuff. That's the kind of stuff it falls into.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Having worked on the other side, some groups get bonuses based on the number of letters they get. I don't think the letters are effective. One thing is, we have passed rules or resolutions in the past for issues directly related to the city, and the legislature watches what we do. Sometimes they react the next day and change the law to stop us from doing what we're doing. You take a democratically controlled City Council and you send a letter to a republican-controlled legislature, and they are probably going to do the opposite. It will have the opposite impact. Anyway --

segments.speaker: Guido Maniscalco
segments.text: I'll leave it.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Councilman Miranda, any new business?

segments.speaker: Charlie Miranda
segments.text: No, sir.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: We're all empathetic with it. Just like all the issues, we know where our politics are at.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: I started washing my clothes on the weekend to save money. The electric bills --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Couple of things. One, thank you, staff, for the support and going through council's responsibility thus far. We see what comes back from the mayor's office on the charter. This has been a long, long road. I mean, months and months and months. Thank you, Hagar. Thank you, Mr. Shelby. Thank you to all the staff and everybody including sam and everybody else that's had a part in this. If you've been paying attention to me, you see my left eye is a little weird. Next week I'm having eye surgery to try to correct it. It's droopy and weird. When you see me next, sam punched me in the eye. [ laughter ]

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: So if you see me and I look really, really awful, that's why. Sam punched me in the eye. Motion to receive and file? Motion from Councilman Miranda. Second from Councilwoman Hurtak.
